title: Are You Blaming Difficult Students For Poor Classroom Management? classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin, marking more than six years of writing SCM, revisits his commitment to telling hard truths about classroom management. He addresses the common teacher justification of blaming a few difficult students for a chaotic classroom, particularly late in the day when a class becomes excitable and unmanageable. While acknowledging this feeling is understandable, Linsin insists that widespread misbehavior is a sign of poor classroom management generally, not the fault of a handful of students. He argues that exceptional classroom managers respond by focusing on comprehensive, class-wide improvement rather than fixating on the most difficult individuals, and that as trust and buy-in spread among the majority, even the toughest students eventually fall in line because they want to belong to something positive. The article frames belonging as the most powerful motivator available to teachers.
points: Blaming a handful of difficult students for classroom-wide chaos, especially late in the day, is a common but flawed narrative among struggling teachers.
Linsin reframes classwide misbehavior as a symptom of poor classroom management overall rather than the cause created by a few students.
Exceptional classroom managers focus on comprehensive, class-wide improvement—covering everything from the physical environment to transitions—rather than targeting a few individuals.
As trust and buy-in spread through the majority of the class, difficult students typically fall in line because they no longer have peers to enable or laugh along with their behavior.
The desire to belong to something bigger than oneself is described as the most powerful motivator a teacher can leverage.
quotes: When I began this blog more than six years ago, I made a commitment to telling the whole truth about classroom management.
But the truth is, this is a sign of poor classroom management, not the cause of it.
If you were to take an exceptional classroom manager and drop them into a class like the one above, they wouldn’t focus on the most difficult students.
It is this comprehensive approach, of consistently applying proven and effective methods, that has the power to transform any classroom, no matter how far gone, from chaotic to peaceful.
They look around and see everyone else behaving and no one to laugh at their silliness. They look around and realize that their behavior is absurd, out of place, and no longer fun and enticing.
They want to be part of something bigger than themselves. We all do. It’s the most powerful motivator in the universe.
